about: Protobuf Studio lets you work with Protocol Buffers binary without installing protoc. You can write or paste a proto3 schema, turn a JSON object into wire-format bytes, decode hex or Base64 bytes back into JSON using a chosen message, and inspect raw bytes with no schema at all. It is aimed at developers debugging gRPC payloads, queue messages and stored blobs, where the question is usually what these bytes actually contain.

Protobuf data is not self-describing. A serialized message is a sequence of tag and value pairs where the tag packs a field number and a wire type, and the names and logical types exist only in the `.proto` file. This is why the tool has two modes: schema-driven encode and decode, which gives you real field names and types, and a schema-free wire inspector, which can only show field numbers, wire types, lengths and candidate values.

The engine is a small hand-written proto3 subset implementation that runs in the page. The README states that no network requests are made and no message content is sent to a server, and that source and payloads live only in the current frame with no local storage. File import is limited to 2 MiB.

It is not a replacement for protoc. It rejects constructs it cannot handle correctly, instead of guessing, so unsupported schemas fail loudly. For text-level inspection of the bytes before decoding, [Hex Studio](/hex-tools/) and [Encoder / Decoder](/encoder-decoder/) are useful companions, and [JSON Tools](/json-tools/) will format the decoded result.

features.title: Schema validation with clear errors
features.body: The parser accepts proto3 messages, nested messages, enums, repeated fields and the scalar types. It checks identifiers, duplicate names, duplicate field numbers, the reserved 19000 to 19999 range and unresolved type names.

features.title: JSON to binary encoding
features.body: Pick a message, supply a JSON object, and get the encoded bytes as hex and Base64. Field names can be written in snake_case or camelCase, and unknown keys are rejected so a typo cannot silently drop data.

features.title: Binary to JSON decoding
features.body: Paste hex (spaces, colons, dashes and underscores are tolerated) or Base64, choose a message, and read the decoded JSON. Enum numbers are shown as names where the schema defines them.

features.title: Schema-free wire inspector
features.body: Lists each field with its byte offset, field number, wire type, byte count and value. Length-delimited fields show up to 24 bytes of hex plus a printable-text preview when the bytes look like text.

features.title: Starter schema from JSON
features.body: Infer a first-draft `.proto` from a JSON sample. Integers become `int32` or `int64`, other numbers become `double`, arrays become `repeated`, and nested objects become nested messages.

features.title: Safety limits
features.body: Nesting is capped at 32 levels, schemas and payloads at 2 MiB, and decoding stops after 100,000 fields. The wire inspector stops at 1,000 fields. Malformed varints and truncated fields produce errors instead of partial output.

reference.title: How the wire format and the tool's type mapping work

blocks.text: Each field starts with a varint tag equal to `(field_number << 3) | wire_type`. Wire type 0 is a varint, 1 is a fixed 8 bytes, 2 is length-delimited (a varint length then that many bytes) and 5 is a fixed 4 bytes. Wire types 3 and 4 (groups) are deprecated and the tool rejects them as invalid tags.

A varint stores seven bits per byte, least significant group first, with the high bit set on every byte except the last. A 64-bit value therefore takes at most ten bytes, and the decoder rejects anything longer. Field 1 with value 150 encodes as `08 96 01`: tag `08` is field 1, wire type 0, and `96 01` is 150.

items: ZigZag encoding for `sint32` and `sint64` maps signed numbers to unsigned ones so small negatives stay small: 0, -1, 1, -2 become 0, 1, 2, 3. A plain negative `int32` or `int64` always uses ten bytes.
Repeated scalar fields (numbers, bools, enums) are written packed: one tag with wire type 2 followed by the values back to back. The decoder accepts packed data and also repeated individual entries.
Repeated strings, bytes and messages are written as one tag-and-length entry per element.
Fields set to `null` or left out are not written, and unknown fields found while decoding are skipped, not reported.
64-bit integers are strings in JSON because JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53 - 1. Passing a unsafe integer as a number gets the error `Use decimal strings for 64-bit integers`.

blocks.text: Proto3 has no field presence for plain scalars: a zero value is indistinguishable from unset. The tool writes any value you supply, including zeros, but a decoder cannot tell whether the sender meant it.

The checker scans for a list of keywords before parsing and refuses the whole schema if it finds `import`, `extend`, `extensions`, `group`, `oneof`, `service`, `rpc`, `option`, `reserved`, `required` or `weak`. It also refuses `syntax = "proto2"`, `map<...>` fields, proto3 `optional` and bracketed field options. Allowed top-level statements are `syntax`, `package`, `message` and `enum`.

Field numbers must be between 1 and 536,870,911 and cannot fall in 19000 to 19999, which the protobuf implementation reserves. Numbers 1 to 15 take a single tag byte, so assign them to the most frequently used fields. Names and numbers are checked for duplicates within each message.

example.title: Round trip a small message and read the bytes

blocks.text: Use this schema in the editor, select message `studio.Person`, and encode the JSON below it.
The output bytes follow the wire layout field by field. Verify against the hex view:

blocks.code:
0a 03 41 6e 61     field 1, length 3, "Ana"
10 96 01           field 2, varint 150
1a 01 61           field 3, length 1, "a"
1a 01 62           field 3, length 1, "b"

blocks.text: Now paste that hex into the decoder with the same message selected and you get the JSON back. To see what the wire inspector does with no schema, run the same hex through it: you will see fields 1 and 3 as length-delimited with a text preview, and field 2 as wire type 0 with value 150, but no names. That gap is exactly the information the schema supplies.

limits: This is not protoc or protobuf.js. Imports, maps, oneof, services, options, proto2 and proto3 optional are rejected, so real-world schemas that use them must be reduced by hand before use here.
Inferred schemas are starter drafts. Field numbers follow the key order in your sample, so they are not stable across edits and must not be applied to a service that already has deployed clients.
Schema-free inspection cannot recover names, distinguish `int32` from `sint32` or a nested message from a string, or know whether a fixed value is a float.
There is no code generation for other languages. Use protoc, buf or your language's plugin for that.
Unknown fields are dropped when decoding with a schema, so a message produced by a newer schema may show fewer fields than it contains. Use the wire inspector to see them.

faq.question: Why are my int64 values strings in JSON?
faq.answer: JavaScript numbers are doubles and cannot hold every 64-bit integer. Using decimal strings preserves exact values, and the tool refuses an unsafe number rather than rounding it.

faq.question: How do I send bytes fields?
faq.answer: Write them as a Base64 string in the JSON input. When decoding, bytes fields are returned as Base64 strings as well.

faq.question: Why does decoding give me fewer fields than I expect?
faq.answer: Fields whose numbers are not in the selected message are skipped silently, as protobuf decoders normally do. Choose the correct message or add the missing fields, or use the wire inspector for a raw listing.

faq.question: Can I decode a gRPC response directly?
faq.answer: A gRPC frame starts with a 1-byte compression flag and a 4-byte length before the protobuf message. Remove those five bytes first, then paste the rest.

faq.question: Does my data leave the browser?
faq.answer: The tool does not send schemas or payloads anywhere and keeps them only in the current page. Clipboard and download actions happen through the host when you request them.
